clinicalPearls: OA is the most common type of arthritis and a leading cause of disability in the elderly; prevalence rises strikingly with age, being uncommon before 40 and highly prevalent after 60 (Harrison 22e p.2949).

Joint involvement is characteristic: hips, knees, first MTP joint, cervical/lumbosacral spine, and in the hands the DIP, PIP, and thumb base; the wrist, elbow, and ankle are usually spared (Harrison 22e p.2949).

Joint pain is primarily activity-related early on, coming on during or just after use and resolving with rest; as disease progresses pain becomes continuous and may be bothersome at night (Harrison 22e p.2952).
Morning stiffness, when present, is usually brief (<30 min), in contrast to the prolonged stiffness (hours) of inflammatory arthritis (Harrison 22e p.2952).
Hand OA produces bony enlargement of the DIP joints (Heberden's nodes) and PIP joints (Bouchard's nodes) (Harrison 22e p.2949).
On hip examination, OA can be detected by loss of internal rotation on passive movement (Harrison 22e p.2953).
Mechanical symptoms (buckling, catching, locking) are common in knee OA and need further evaluation for internal derangement only when they follow an acute knee injury (Harrison 22e p.2952).
Osteophytes are an important radiographic hallmark of OA, along with joint-space narrowing reflecting cartilage loss (Harrison 22e pp.2952-2953).
harrison.pathophysiology: OA is joint failure in which all joint structures undergo pathologic change. The pathologic hallmark is focal, initially nonuniform loss of hyaline articular cartilage, accompanied by thickening and sclerosis of the subchondral bony plate, marginal osteophyte outgrowth, stretching of the articular capsule, variable synovitis, and weakness of muscles bridging the joint (meniscal degeneration occurs in knees). Disease begins with joint injury when protective mechanisms (joint capsule/ligaments, bridging muscle, sensory afferents, underlying bone, and synovial-fluid lubrication via hyaluronic acid and lubricin) fail. Cartilage shows depletion of aggrecan and loss/unfurling of type 2 collagen, losing compressive stiffness; chondrocytes shift toward catabolism, producing matrix-degrading enzymes (MMPs, ADAMTS-5). Local inflammation (including mechanoinflammation), with cytokines, alarmins/DAMPs, and growth factors (BMP-2, TGF-beta drive osteophytes; VEGF drives vascular invasion), accelerates progression. Risk reflects the balance between joint vulnerability (age, female sex, genetics such as GDF5, prior damage, malalignment, bridging-muscle weakness, high bone density) and joint loading (obesity, occupational/repetitive use, major injury) (Harrison 22e pp.2949-2952).
additionalDifferentials: Inflammatory arthritis (suggested by prolonged morning stiffness and involvement of many joints)
Bursitis (anserine bursitis medial/distal to the knee; trochanteric bursitis lateral to the hip)
Internal derangement of the knee (anterior cruciate ligament or meniscal tear), especially after acute injury
infectionMimics: Septic arthritis (consider when synovial fluid white count is elevated/inflammatory)
nonInfectiousMimics: Gout and pseudogout (crystal arthritis; suggested by synovial fluid white count >1000/uL with identifiable crystals)
Rheumatoid arthritis and other inflammatory arthritides
additionalInvestigations: No blood tests are routinely indicated unless symptoms or signs suggest inflammatory arthritis (Harrison 22e p.2953).

Synovial fluid examination is often more helpful diagnostically than x-ray; a white count >1000/uL suggests inflammatory arthritis, gout, or pseudogout, the latter two confirmed by crystals (Harrison 22e p.2953).

Radiographs are not routinely indicated; order only when pain and findings are atypical of OA or when pain persists after effective treatment. Imaging findings correlate poorly with pain, and x-rays may be normal in early disease (insensitive to cartilage loss) (Harrison 22e p.2953).

MRI is not indicated in the diagnostic workup; meniscal tears and cartilage/bone lesions are common both in OA and in older persons without joint pain, and MRI findings rarely warrant a change in therapy (Harrison 22e p.2953).
redFlags: Prominent nocturnal pain in the absence of end-stage OA merits a distinct workup (Harrison 22e p.2953).
Prolonged morning stiffness with many joints affected suggests inflammatory arthritis rather than OA (Harrison 22e p.2952).
Mechanical symptoms (buckling, catching, locking) developing after an acute knee injury warrant evaluation for internal derangement (Harrison 22e p.2952).
harrison.prognosis: OA is a chronic, generally progressive disorder of the elderly whose high prevalence and impact on physical function make it a leading cause of disability. Severely malaligned knees may be destined to progress regardless of other risk factors, whereas weight loss greater than 10% of body weight reduces cartilage loss and, in most affected persons, alleviates pain (Harrison 22e pp.2949-2952).
pitfalls: Distinguish OA from rheumatoid (and other inflammatory) arthritis, crystal arthritis (gout/pseudogout), and septic arthritis; prolonged morning stiffness, systemic features, and an inflammatory synovial fluid white count point away from OA.
Do not rely on radiographs to gauge symptom severity: x-ray changes correlate poorly with pain, and films may be normal in early disease.
Many persons with x-ray or MRI evidence of OA have no joint symptoms, so structural findings alone do not establish symptomatic OA.
Back pain and neck pain are not tied to x-ray findings of spinal OA and are evaluated separately.
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison's chapter 383 does not present a single formal grading scale; OA is characterized clinically along a spectrum from early, episodic activity-related pain with brief morning stiffness to advanced/end-stage disease with continuous and nocturnal pain. The chapter references the WOMAC index as a patient-reported outcome measure of pain, stiffness, and function (Harrison 22e p.2952).
management: Core non-pharmacological management with patient education, individualised exercise including muscle strengthening and aerobic activity, and weight loss in the overweight
Topical non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs first-line, with oral NSAIDs at the lowest effective dose, adjunctive analgesia and consideration of duloxetine for persistent pain
Intra-articular corticosteroid injection for painful flares of the affected joint
Physical adjuncts such as walking aids, appropriate footwear and braces to offload and support symptomatic joints
Referral for joint replacement or other surgery in end-stage disease with refractory pain and functional limitation
Regular review of symptoms, function and treatment tolerability, with attention to comorbidities affecting drug choice
